books.section: Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

options.misconception: Background: Reconstruction ended in 1877, and railroad consolidation was a national economic process, not a Southern political one.

The rise of giant corporations that dominated whole industries

rationales.A: Background: Reconstruction ended in 1877, and railroad consolidation was a national economic process, not part of the South's return to the Union.
rationales.B: Background: the Ghost Dance was spiritual resistance to reservation life. It answered the loss of land and the buffalo, not railroad finance.
rationales.C: The railroad barons were the first of the giants. Background: their consolidation — buying rivals, controlling every step — became the model for trusts in oil, steel, and sugar.
rationales.D: Background: the Homestead Act passed in 1862, before this period began, and it offered land to settlers rather than building corporate power.
rationales.general:
Follow the pattern, not the single villain: Vanderbilt is one example of a bigger habit.
1. Name what Vanderbilt did. Background: he bought rivals and controlled the lines, the freight, and the tolls.
2. Ask where else that habit appears. Background: oil, steel, and sugar all grew the same way, into trusts.
3. Name the feature. Giant corporations dominating whole industries, with railroads as the model.
Remember: when one industry's trick shows up everywhere, it is the period's pattern, not one man's scheme.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Joseph Keppler, Puck, 1879, public domain.
stem: The power the cartoon attacks grew out of developments that also shaped which of the following features of the period?

stimulus.source_note: Joseph Keppler, 'The Modern Colossus of (Rail) Roads,' Puck magazine, 1879. Public domain. Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Modern_Colossus_of_Rail_Roads_-_Keppler_1879.jpg
stimulus.text: The cartoon shows railroad magnate William Henry Vanderbilt as a giant straddling the nation, holding the strings that control the railroads below him. Two smaller figures, railroad men Jay Gould and Cyrus Field, stand beneath his feet. A sign at his feet reads: 'All freight seeking the seaboard MUST pass here and pay any tolls WE DEMAND.'
